characters.name: The Elder
characters.perkNote: Self-designated only as "the elder" in the text (matching 2 John 1:1). Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle/Evangelist, the same traditional author as 1 John and 2 John and, by further tradition, the Gospel of John and Revelation — but 3 John itself never states this name, so it is flagged as tradition, not textual fact.

verses.note: The elder writes to the "wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth."
Wishes Gaius prosperity and health, matching the prosperity of his soul.
Rejoices greatly when brethren came and testified of the truth in Gaius, that he walks in the truth.
Says he has no greater joy than hearing that his "children" walk in truth.
States that such traveling brethren ought to be received, and that he wrote to the church — but Diotrephes, who loves preeminence, receiveth us not.

Says that if he comes he will remember Diotrephes' deeds: prating against us (the elder and his companions) with malicious words, refusing to receive the brethren himself, forbidding others who would, and casting them out of the church.
Personally bears record that Demetrius' good report is true.
Has many things to write but prefers not to use ink and pen; trusts he will shortly see Gaius and speak face to face; sends peace and greetings from friends.

funFacts: Uses the exact phrase "ink and pen" (3 John 1:13) to describe the physical act of letter-writing he is choosing NOT to rely on, preferring a face-to-face visit instead.
Opens 2 John with the identical self-designation "the elder," which is part of why the two short letters are traditionally attributed to the same author.

characters.name: Gaius
characters.perkNote: Distinct from other New Testament men named Gaius (of Corinth, Romans 16:23 / 1 Corinthians 1:14; of Macedonia, Acts 19:29; of Derbe, Acts 20:4) — the text of 3 John does not identify this Gaius with any of them.

verses.note: Addressed as "the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth."
The elder wishes he may prosper and be in health, even as his soul prospereth.
Brethren testified that he walks in the truth; called one of the elder's spiritual "children."
Commended for doing faithfully whatever he does for the brethren and for strangers, whose testimony of his charity reached the church.
Urged to help the traveling brethren forward on their journey "after a godly sort."
Exhorted by the elder to follow that which is good, and not that which is evil: "he that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God," in contrast to Diotrephes' example.

characters.name: Diotrephes

verses.note: Described as loving to have the preeminence among the brethren; does not receive the elder or his authority.

The elder will remember his deeds if he comes: prating against us (the elder) with malicious words, refusing to receive the brethren himself, forbidding others who would, and casting them out of the church.

funFacts: The only individual in the New Testament described explicitly as "loving to have the preeminence" (3 John 1:9). The text gives no other biographical detail (no genealogy, prior history, or stated outcome) for him beyond this letter.

characters.name: Demetrius
characters.perkNote: Distinct from Demetrius the silversmith of Ephesus (Acts 19:24-41), who incited a riot against Paul — the text draws no connection between the two men.

verses.note: Has good report of all men, and of the truth itself; the elder and others also bear record, and that record is true.

characters.name: The Brethren and Strangers
characters.perkNote: A collective group of traveling missionaries, not individually named or differentiated in the text — treated as one entry rather than invented individuals, per the established methodology.

verses.note: Received hospitality from Gaius as "brethren" and "strangers"; bore witness of his charity before the church.
Went forth for the Name's sake, taking nothing of the Gentiles.
The elder states such travelers ought to be received, so that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

friends_greeting.note: "Our friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name" — unnamed collective well-wishers on both ends of the correspondence, not individually identified in the text.

spiritual_children.note: "My children" — the elder's spiritual converts/disciples in general, not named individuals; no biological family is mentioned for the elder anywhere in this letter.

the_church.note: "The church" the elder wrote to, and from which Diotrephes casts out willing brethren — the congregation/institution itself, not a person, so kept out of the character list.

notes: 3 John is the shortest book in the New Testament — one chapter, 14 verses — a private letter from "the elder" to a beloved friend, Gaius, commending his hospitality toward traveling missionaries, warning against a self-aggrandizing local figure named Diotrephes who abuses his standing to block that hospitality and expel dissenters, and closing with a brief commendation of a third man, Demetrius. All three named individuals plus the letter's own author-voice ("the elder") are genuinely person-driven in miniature, so this book uses four person-type manager tiers and no law/theme tiers — there is no doctrinal or legal content here, only personal exhortation and church-politics narrative in miniature. The one collective figure worth tracking, "the brethren and strangers" whom Gaius supported and whose testimony of his charity reached the elder, is folded into a single submanager under Gaius (loyalty-boost) rather than invented as individually named people, since the text never differentiates them. Naming-collision flags: this Gaius is not identified in the text with the Gaius of Corinth (Romans 16:23, 1 Corinthians 1:14), Macedonia (Acts 19:29), or Derbe (Acts 20:4); this Demetrius is not identified with the silversmith of Acts 19:24-41; and "the elder" is only ever self-designated that way in the text (matching 2 John 1:1) — the traditional identification with John the Apostle/Evangelist is noted as tradition, not asserted as textual fact. No genealogy data (parents/spouses/children) is stated anywhere in this book for any figure, so every genealogy field is empty/null; ageEvents are empty across the board for the same reason — this is a personal letter, not a narrative with biographical detail. Schema/correction notes from the adversarial fact-check pass: the elder's and Diotrephes' 3 John 1:10 notes were corrected — the KJV text reads "prating against us" (the elder speaking of himself and his companions), not "against him," and the ambiguous original phrasing could be misread as Diotrephes prating against himself; Diotrephes' funFact was trimmed to remove outside historical/interpretive commentary ("early example of local-church authority conflict") not stated in the text itself, per this project's descriptive-not-doctrinal rule; 3 John 1:11's second clause ("he that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God") was folded into Gaius's existing 1:11 verse note alongside the first clause (the exhortation to follow good, not evil), since both clauses form one continuous address to him; and the notes field no longer asserts an unconfirmed "exactly like Philemon" precedent, since Philemon has not yet been indexed in this project's record.
